```{r}
#| label: setup
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
library(CanadaForestAllometry)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

DBH–height (`hd_*()`) models predict **total tree height (m)** from diameter at
breast height (DBH, cm, measured at 1.3 m). They are typically used to fill in
heights of trees that were not measured, before applying a volume or biomass
model that requires height.

Many published DBH–height models need more than DBH: stand-level predictors
such as basal area, stems per hectare or dominant height, climate normals, or
ecological classification codes. Each source also defines these predictors
differently (size thresholds, all-species vs species-specific totals,
dominant-height definitions). For this reason:

- each model is a separate function whose arguments are exactly the
  predictors that model uses;
- there is **no automatic model selection** (unlike `vol()`): you choose the
  model, and a missing required predictor is an error, never replaced by a
  proxy;
- a registry and two helper functions let you find which models suit your
  data, and what each predictor means in the source publication.

# DBH–height models included in the package

```{r}
#| label: hd-model-list
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
reg <- CanadaForestAllometry:::hd_model_registry_species()

fmt_args <- function(x) {
  if (length(x) == 0L) "—" else paste0("`", x, "`", collapse = ", ")
}

reg_fun <- reg |>
  dplyr::group_by(.data$engine) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    reference = dplyr::first(.data$reference),
    province_scope = paste(sort(unique(unlist(.data$province_scope))), collapse = ", "),
    stand_origin = dplyr::first(.data$stand_origin),
    variants = paste0("`", .data$model_id, "`", collapse = ", "),
    n_species = max(.data$n_species),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

origin_text <- c(
  natural = "natural stands",
  plantation = "plantations",
  both = "natural stands and plantations"
)

for (i in seq_len(nrow(reg_fun))) {
  x <- reg_fun[i, ]
  cat(
    "- [`", x$engine, "()`](../reference/", x$engine, ".html) [", x$reference, "]. ",
    "Coverage: ", x$province_scope, ", ", origin_text[[x$stand_origin]], ". ",
    x$n_species, " species. Model ID(s): ", x$variants, ".\n",
    sep = ""
  )
}
```

The registry has one row per model **variant**. Some functions implement
several variants: `hd_eslamdoust2026()` chooses M4 (DBH only) or M5 (with
stand variables) from the predictors you supply, and `hd_auger2025()` uses an
explicit `variant` argument because its variants need different inputs.

```{r}
#| label: hd-registry-table
#| echo: false
reg |>
  dplyr::transmute(
    `Model ID` = paste0("`", .data$model_id, "`"),
    Function = paste0("`", .data$engine, "()`"),
    Jurisdiction = vapply(.data$province_scope, paste, character(1), collapse = ", "),
    Origin = .data$stand_origin,
    `Required predictors` = vapply(.data$required_predictors, fmt_args, character(1)),
    `Optional predictors` = vapply(.data$optional_predictors, fmt_args, character(1)),
    Species = .data$n_species
  ) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

# Finding a model for your data

`hd_model_registry()` returns the full metadata table (model form, region
argument, whether calibration information is published, etc.):

```{r}
hd_model_registry() |>
  dplyr::select(model_id, engine, province_scope, equation_family, required_predictors)
```

`find_hd_models()` filters the registry by jurisdiction and species, and
reports which required predictors each candidate needs that you do not have.
Models with missing predictors are kept as "near misses", so you can see what
extra data would make them usable:

```{r}
find_hd_models(
  jurisdiction = "ON",
  species = "PICE.MAR",
  available = c("DBH", "BA", "TPH")
) |>
  dplyr::select(model_id, usable, missing_predictors)
```

Here `hd_sharmaparton2007()` covers black spruce in Ontario but also needs
dominant height (`HDOM`). Names in `available` are the `hd_*()` argument names
and are case-sensitive.

`get_hd_model_info()` returns the registry entry of one model, its species
coverage, and its predictor table:

```{r}
info <- get_hd_model_info("sharmaparton2007")
info$species
info$predictors
```

# Predictors

Predictor arguments follow a shared vocabulary, with upper-case acronyms and
lower-case words. A shared name is used only when the source's quantity fits
it; the exact definition (size threshold, species basis, dominant-height
definition) is **model-specific** and is given in each function's help page
and in the table below.

| Argument | Level | Units | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `DBH` | tree | cm | Diameter at breast height (1.3 m) |
| `species` | tree | NFI code | Species code, e.g. `PICE.MAR` |
| `BA` | plot | m²/ha | Stand basal area |
| `TPH` | plot | stems/ha | Stand density |
| `HDOM` | plot | m | Dominant (or dominant and codominant) height |
| `QMD` | plot | cm | Quadratic mean DBH |
| region / classification | plot | code | Model-specific names, e.g. `natural_subregion` (AB), `SDOM`, `MP`, `VP` (QC) |

Plot-level predictors can be given as a single value (recycled to all trees)
or as one value per tree. The package does not compute stand variables from
tree lists, because each source defines them differently: compute `BA`,
`TPH`, `HDOM`, etc. following the definition of the model you use.

Predictor definitions for every implemented model, as given in the source
publication (with page or table):

```{r}
#| label: hd-predictor-table
#| echo: false
purrr::map(
  hd_model_registry()$model_id,
  function(id) {
    get_hd_model_info(id)$predictors |>
      dplyr::mutate(model_id = id, .before = 1)
  }
) |>
  purrr::list_rbind() |>
  dplyr::transmute(
    `Model ID` = paste0("`", .data$model_id, "`"),
    Argument = paste0("`", .data$arg, "`"),
    Level = .data$level,
    Units = .data$units,
    Required = ifelse(.data$required, "yes", "no"),
    Definition = .data$definition,
    Source = .data$source_locator
  ) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

For `hd_auger2016()`, the optional predictors are required only for the
species whose model uses them; see `?hd_auger2016` and the source for the
per-species predictor sets.

# Using the models

All `hd_*()` functions are vectorized, return a tibble with a `height` column
(m), and can be used directly inside `dplyr::mutate()`:

```{r}
#| message: false
trees <- tibble::tibble(
  plot = c(1, 1, 1, 2, 2),
  DBH = c(12, 25, 18, 30, 9),
  species = c("PICE.MAR", "PINU.BAN", "POPU.TRE", "PICE.GLA", "ABIE.BAL"),
  HDOM = c(16, 16, 16, 22, 22),
  BA = c(30, 30, 30, 18, 18),
  TPH = c(3000, 3000, 3000, 1200, 1200)
)

trees |>
  dplyr::mutate(hd_sharmaparton2007(DBH, species, HDOM = HDOM, BA = BA, TPH = TPH))
```

A model using DBH only:

```{r}
#| message: false
trees |>
  dplyr::mutate(hd_huang2016(DBH, species))
```

## Variants

When a source defines a hierarchy of models, the variant is chosen from the
inputs you supply and reported once per session with a message. For example,
`hd_huang2016()` uses the provincial models unless `natural_subregion` is
given, and `hd_eslamdoust2026()` uses M5 only when `HDOM`, `BA` and `TPH` are
all supplied (supplying only some of them is an error). Set
`keep_model_id = TRUE` to return the variant used for each tree:

```{r}
hd_eslamdoust2026(
  DBH = c(15, 30),
  species = c("ACER.SAH", "PINU.STR"),
  HDOM = 22, BA = 30, TPH = 1200,
  keep_model_id = TRUE
)
```

When variants need different inputs, the variant is chosen explicitly:

```{r}
hd_auger2025(
  DBH = c(6, 9, 12),
  species = "PICE.MAR",
  variant = "dominant",
  HDOM = 9, dominant_DBH = 11
)
```

## Missing values and applicability limits

Rows with `NA` in a required input return `NA` height (no error), so the
functions can be applied to tree lists with incomplete data. Inputs outside
the range of the source's fitting data are still computed, and a single
warning lists the affected rows:

```{r}
hd_sharmaparton2007(
  DBH = c(20, NA, 80),
  species = "PICE.MAR",
  HDOM = 20, BA = 25, TPH = 2500
)
```

# Population-level vs calibrated prediction

Most DBH–height models are fitted as mixed-effects models with plot-level
random effects. The `hd_*()` functions return **population-level**
predictions: the fixed effects recommended by the source for trees in plots
without height measurements, with random effects set to zero. For nonlinear
mixed models this is the curve of a "typical" plot with the supplied
predictors, not the mean over plots.

If some trees in a plot have measured heights, a model can be **calibrated**
to that plot by predicting its random effects from the measured heights. This
usually improves predictions considerably, but it is not implemented yet. The
`calibration_published` column of `hd_model_registry()` indicates whether the
source publishes the variance components needed for it:

```{r}
hd_model_registry() |>
  dplyr::select(model_id, prediction_types, calibration_published)
```

# Model curves

The figures below show population-level DBH–height curves for each model and
species. For models with stand-level predictors, curves are shown for the
reference plot values stated with each figure; heights for other plots can
differ substantially. Curves are drawn over a common DBH range and may extend
beyond the fitting data of a species.

```{r}
#| label: hd-curve-helper
#| echo: false
plot_hd_curves <- function(data, colour = NULL, colour_lab = NULL, ncol = 4) {
  p <- ggplot2::ggplot(
    data,
    ggplot2::aes(x = .data$DBH, y = .data$height)
  )
  if (is.null(colour)) {
    p <- p + ggplot2::geom_line(linewidth = 0.6)
  } else {
    p <- p +
      ggplot2::geom_line(
        ggplot2::aes(colour = factor(.data[[colour]])),
        linewidth = 0.6
      ) +
      ggplot2::labs(colour = colour_lab)
  }
  p +
    ggplot2::facet_wrap(ggplot2::vars(.data$species), ncol = ncol) +
    ggplot2::labs(x = "DBH (cm)", y = "Height (m)") +
    ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
    ggplot2::theme(legend.position = "bottom")
}

hd_species <- function(model_id) get_hd_model_info(model_id)$species

fig_height <- function(n_species, ncol = 4) 1.0 + 2.0 * ceiling(n_species / ncol)
```

## `hd_huang2016()`

Alberta [@Huang2016hd]. Provincial models (no `natural_subregion`).

```{r}
#| label: fig-huang2016
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: !expr fig_height(length(hd_species("huang2016")))
grid <- tidyr::expand_grid(species = hd_species("huang2016"), DBH = seq(1, 60, by = 1))
grid$height <- hd_huang2016(grid$DBH, grid$species)$height
plot_hd_curves(grid)
```

## `hd_sharmaparton2007()`

Northern Ontario boreal [@SharmaParton2007]. `BA` = 25 m²/ha and
`TPH` = 2,500 stems/ha, for several dominant heights (`HDOM`), as in Fig. 2 of
the source.

```{r}
#| label: fig-sharmaparton2007
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: !expr fig_height(length(hd_species("sharmaparton2007"))) + 0.5
grid <- tidyr::expand_grid(
  species = hd_species("sharmaparton2007"),
  HDOM = c(10, 15, 20, 25),
  DBH = seq(1, 60, by = 1)
)
grid$height <- hd_sharmaparton2007(
  grid$DBH, grid$species, HDOM = grid$HDOM, BA = 25, TPH = 2500
)$height
plot_hd_curves(grid, colour = "HDOM", colour_lab = "HDOM (m)")
```

## `hd_eslamdoust2026()`

Ontario boreal and Great Lakes–St. Lawrence forests [@Eslamdoust2026]. M4
(DBH only) and M5 with `HDOM` = 20 m, `BA` = 25 m²/ha and
`TPH` = 1,500 stems/ha.

```{r}
#| label: fig-eslamdoust2026
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: !expr fig_height(length(hd_species("eslamdoust2026_m4"))) + 0.5
grid <- tidyr::expand_grid(
  species = hd_species("eslamdoust2026_m4"),
  DBH = seq(1, 60, by = 1)
)
m4 <- dplyr::mutate(grid, model = "M4", height = hd_eslamdoust2026(DBH, species)$height)
m5 <- dplyr::mutate(
  grid,
  model = "M5",
  height = hd_eslamdoust2026(DBH, species, HDOM = 20, BA = 25, TPH = 1500)$height
)
plot_hd_curves(dplyr::bind_rows(m4, m5), colour = "model", colour_lab = "Model")
```

## `hd_auger2016()`

Québec, 27 species [@Auger2016]. Reference plot: `BA` = 20 m²/ha,
`QMD` = 20 cm, `SDOM` = `"4est"`, `MP` = `"2"`, `VP` = `"MS2"`,
`TMOY` = 2 °C, `PTOT` = 1,000 mm, `altitude` = 300 m, `disturbance` =
`"none"` (each species uses only the predictors in its model). The source
advises against use for trees with DBH < 9 cm, so curves start at 9 cm.

```{r}
#| label: fig-auger2016
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: !expr fig_height(length(hd_species("auger2016")), ncol = 5)
grid <- tidyr::expand_grid(species = hd_species("auger2016"), DBH = seq(9, 60, by = 1))
grid$height <- hd_auger2016(
  grid$DBH, grid$species,
  BA = 20, QMD = 20, SDOM = "4est", MP = "2", VP = "MS2",
  TMOY = 2, PTOT = 1000, altitude = 300, disturbance = "none"
)$height
plot_hd_curves(grid, ncol = 5)
```

## `hd_auger2025()`

Québec black spruce and jack pine **plantations** [@Auger2025]. The three
variants: DBH only, plot mean DBH (`mean_DBH` = 12 cm), and dominant height
and DBH (`HDOM` = 12 m, `dominant_DBH` = 16 cm). Curves are limited to the
calibration DBH range of each species.

```{r}
#| label: fig-auger2025
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.8
dbh_max <- CanadaForestAllometry:::get_params_tbl("parameters_hd_Auger2025") |>
  dplyr::filter(.data$variant == "dbh") |>
  dplyr::select("Species", "DBH_max")
grid <- tidyr::expand_grid(species = dbh_max$Species, DBH = seq(0.5, 40, by = 0.5)) |>
  dplyr::left_join(dbh_max, by = c(species = "Species")) |>
  dplyr::filter(.data$DBH <= .data$DBH_max)
v_dbh <- dplyr::mutate(
  grid,
  variant = "dbh",
  height = hd_auger2025(DBH, species)$height
)
v_mean <- dplyr::mutate(
  grid,
  variant = "plot_mean_dbh",
  height = hd_auger2025(DBH, species, variant = "plot_mean_dbh", mean_DBH = 12)$height
)
v_dom <- dplyr::mutate(
  grid,
  variant = "dominant",
  height = hd_auger2025(
    DBH, species, variant = "dominant", HDOM = 12, dominant_DBH = 16
  )$height
)
plot_hd_curves(
  dplyr::bind_rows(v_dbh, v_mean, v_dom),
  colour = "variant", colour_lab = "Variant", ncol = 2
)
```
